claims.text: Watt's Delhi exhibition catalogue lists carving, inlaying, veneering, painting and lacquering as the ways wood was ornamented in Indian architecture, furniture and cabinet work.

quotes.quote: As met with in architecture, furniture and cabinet work, wood is ornamented in various ways such as by carving, inlaying, veneering, painting,- lacquering, etc.

claims.text: Watt judged that no aspect of Indian art had so much to teach the student as woodwork, an art of vast antiquity.

quotes.quote: no aspect of Indian Art can have so much to teacji the student as that of wood-work. It has a vast antiquity

claims.text: The turner (kharádi) with his lathe was met with in every village of India and held an assured position in the community.

quotes.locator: Class VI, Division 26, Lac-ware of India, p. 211
quotes.quote: The turner [kharddi) with his lathe is met with in every village of India and has an assured position in the community.
The kharádi (turner) is found in every town and large village.

claims.text: Village turners prepared toys, nests of boxes, bed-posts, hookah mouthpieces and similar turned articles, Watt recorded.

quotes.locator: Class VI, Division 26, Lac-ware of India, p. 211
quotes.quote: He prepares toys, nests of boxes, bed-posts, pdn ddns, hukka mouth-pieces, and the like.

claims.text: Watt regarded inlaying as an art rarely practised by itself, with no special craft and designs like those of carving, though a few centres had long been reputed for expert inlayers.

quotes.quote: Inlaying, for example, is an art rarely practised by itself. There is no special craft devoted to it, and the designs adopted differ in no essential from those of carving.
At the same time there are a few centres that have for long years past enjoyed the reputation of having expert inlayers

claims.text: The Salar Jung Museum calls wood carving an ancient art of India, where wood traditionally made house posts, rafters, yokes, ploughs, toys, planks and furniture.

quotes.quote: Wood carving is an ancient art of India. Though traditionally wood has been used for making home posts, rafters, yokes, ploughs, toys, planks, furniture among others

claims.text: The FAO study defines lac-turnery as turning wood on the lathe, and lacquerware as the lacquered wooden items it produces in and around Channapatna.

quotes.quote: Lac-turnery, the art of turning the wood on the lathe

Lacquerware refers to a wide variety of lacquered wooden items which are prepared through the process of lac-turnery, an indigenous traditional handicraft practiced in and around the town of Channapatna.

claims.text: Watt called lac-turnery an essentially Indian craft and noted that lac was also extensively used to decorate metal and ivory work.

quotes.quote: The craft of lac-turnery is essentially Indian

quotes.locator: Class VI, Division 26, Lac-ware of India, p. 211
quotes.quote: lac is extensively employed as a decorative material in the metal and ivory crafts as well as in that of wood-turnery

claims.text: Watt observed that the wood-carvers and stone-carvers of India belonged to one and the same caste.

quotes.quote: the circumstance that the wood and stone-carvers belong to one and the same caste

claims.text: A tradition in both Peshawar and Rangoon holds that wood-carving originated in connection with boat-building.

quotes.quote: Both in Peshawar in the extreme north of India and Rangoon in further India, the tradition exists that wood-carving originated in connection with boat-building

claims.text: The Salar Jung Museum notes that Emperor Ashoka's palace at Pataliputra and the grand temple at Bodh Gaya were made in wood.

quotes.quote: Emperor Ashoka's palace at Pataliputra was made in wood, and the grand temple at Bodh Gaya as well.

claims.text: The Salar Jung Museum's story says the ancient Indian woodworker made war chariots as well as furniture, doors and panels, and that the Rigveda names him sutradhar.

quotes.quote: In ancient India, the wood-worker made war chariots in addition to furniture, doors and panels. The Rigveda mentions him as sutradhar who was also the charioteer of the chariot he made.

claims.text: The sixth-century Brihat Sanhita lists sal, sandalwood and teak among the woods Hindus most esteemed for furniture, but not tun or shisham.

quotes.locator: Chapter V, Implements and Material, p. 13
quotes.quote: In the Brihat Sanhita, a celebrated work on astronomy dating from the sixth century A. D., a list is given of the kinds of wood most esteemed by Hindus for furniture.

quotes.locator: Chapter V, Implements and Material, p. 13
quotes.quote: Sdl, sandalwood, and teak are mentioned, but tun and shisham, which are used so generally nowadays, are not included.

claims.text: Rules in the Silpa Sastra and Puranas barred carpenters from timber of trees struck by lightning, felled by floods, storms or elephants, fallen southward, or grown on burial grounds.

quotes.locator: Chapter V, Implements and Material, p. 13
quotes.quote: there is a curious collection of forgotten lore in the Silpa Sastra and the Puranas, which imposes certain rules in the selection and felling of trees

quotes.locator: Chapter V, Implements and Material, p. 13
quotes.quote: the timber of trees which have been struck by lightning or borne down by inundations, storms or elephants, or which have fallen towards the south quarter, or which grow on burial-grounds should not be used by carpenters

claims.text: An account quoted by Thurston says Canara's hereditary carvers had a shastram of their own defining which woods suit rough or delicate carving and when and where to fell them.

quotes.locator: Monograph, p. 7, quoting the Calcutta Review
quotes.quote: These hereditary carvers had a shastram or science of their own, which, with wonderful exactitude, and the keenest botanical knowledge, defined and described the various kinds of wood suitable for rough or delicate carving, the age, season, and locality in which these woods ought to be felled

claims.text: Maffey judged that no craft had suffered more than wood-carving, once used by the nobility to embellish houses with carved verandahs, balconies and doors.

quotes.locator: Chapter II, Decline of Wood-Carving, p. 3
quotes.quote: No craft has suffered more than wood-carving. Formerly the nobility and well-to-do citizens took delight in embellishing their houses

quotes.locator: Chapter II, Decline of Wood-Carving, p. 4
quotes.quote: with carved verandahs and balconies. All the chief entrances were filled with massive carved doors.

claims.text: Maffey reported that in Lower Bengal the end had already come and wood-carving was practically extinct.

quotes.locator: Chapter II, Decline of Wood-Carving, p. 5
quotes.quote: In Lower Bengal the end has already come, and wood-carving is practically extinct.

claims.text: Wood-carving at Pilibhit is said to have been introduced in 1764, when a Delhi stone-cutter's pupils extended the art to the abundant local shisham.

quotes.quote: It is said to have been introduced in 1764 by Hdfiz Rahmat Khan, who summoned a skilful stone-cutter from Delhi to direct the ornamentation of the Juma Masjid then under construction.
In the hands of his pupils the art was extended to wood, a primary cause being the natural abundance of shisham wood.

claims.text: Nagina's ebony work grew from gunstocks, charpai legs and masnads carved by local lohars, and attracted European attention only about thirty years before Maffey wrote.

quotes.quote: For some generations the Nagina lohdrs had been in the habit of making gunstocks, chdrpdi legs, and masnads of ebony and adorning them with a superficial floral carving to suit native taste.
Not until about thirty years ago did the industry attract European attention.

claims.text: Maffey wrote that Mainpuri's tarkashi was in the hands of a Hindu family whose forefathers migrated from Rajputana with a Chauhan chief in the fourteenth century.

quotes.quote: The art is in the hands of a Hindu family of g'wasi-Brdhmanical pretensions, whose forefathers migrated from Rdjputdna in the train of a Chauhan chief in the fourteenth century and settled at Mainpuri.

claims.text: In an oral narrative recorded by F. S. Growse, a thirteenth-century Rajputana chieftain is said to have migrated to present-day Uttar Pradesh with decorative artisans.

quotes.quote: FS Growse, a colonial administrator stationed in Mainpuri in the 1860s, records an oral narrative in which a thirteenth-century chieftain from Rajputana (present-day Rajasthan) is said to have migrated to present-day Uttar Pradesh, bringing with him a group of decorative artisans

claims.text: According to Watt, it would appear that sadeli marquetry came to India from Persia (Shiraz) through Sind, perhaps 300 years or so before he wrote.

quotes.quote: It would appear that the art came to India from Persia (Shiraz) through Sind, perhaps 300 years or so ago.

claims.text: Sadeli marquetry was first acquired by Hindus and only later taught to the Parsis, Watt recorded.

quotes.quote: It was first acquired by the Hindus and then subsequently taught to the Parsis.

claims.text: The village of Etikoppaka in Andhra Pradesh has been known for over two centuries for its coloured, lac-coated turned wooden objects.

quotes.quote: The small village of Etikoppaka in Andhra Pradesh has been known for its coloured lac coated turned wood objects for over two centuries.

claims.text: Lac was known in the subcontinent from at least the first millennium BCE and is mentioned in the Atharvaveda, Panini's Astadhyayi and the Mahabharata.

quotes.quote: Lac was known in the subcontinent from at least the first millennium BCE. It is mentioned in three texts from the period: the Atharvaveda, the Astadhyayi of Panini, and the Mahabharata

It is mentioned in three texts from the period: the Atharvaveda, the Astadhyayi of Panini, and the Mahabharata, where the Pandavas are almost killed in a flammable building made of lac resin and ghee.

claims.text: Pinjra work appears in records of Akbar's reign (1556-1605), and the Ain-i-Akbari suggests the craft was by then highly developed and valued.

quotes.quote: Pinjra work appears in historical documents during the reign of the Mughal emperor Akbar (r. 1556-1605); the Ain-i-Akbari, written by his grand vizier Abul Fazl, suggests that the craft had become highly developed and valued by this time.

claims.text: Thrones and state chairs were made in India from the most ancient times and were usually named after the animal or chief object they portrayed.

quotes.quote: Thrones Thrones, and State-chairs have, however, been made from the most ancient times and are usually named after the animal or chief object portrayed

claims.text: Watt recorded that chairs and sofas were a modern introduction in India, where low settees (chaukis) and reed stools were in demand in some parts.

quotes.quote: In some parts of the country low settees {chaukis) and reed stools {?nordhs) are in demand but chairs and sofas are of modern introduction.

claims.text: Watt saw European ideas of comfort steadily creeping into everyday Indian life, creating a demand for household furnishing.

quotes.quote: European ideas of comfort are steadily creeping into the every-day life of the people and accordingly a demand for household furnishing has set in

claims.text: Wood-carving was first started at the Madras School of Arts in 1877 in a desultory way, and its department ornamented European furniture, mostly in teak and blackwood (Dalbergia latifolia).

quotes.quote: Wood-carving was first started in 1877 in a desultory kind of way
Throughout the whole period of its existence the wood-carving department of the school has been devoted to the ornamentation of European furniture.
the great bulk of the work done in the school has been in teakwood, and blackwood or 'rosewood' (Dalbergia latifolia), more particularly the latter.

claims.text: The best ancient teak carvings of Mysore were consumed in the fire of February 1897, which burned the most ornate frontage of the old palace.

quotes.quote: The best specimens of the ancient teak carvings of Mysore were consumed in the fire of February 1897, which reduced to ashes the frontage and most ornate portion of the 'old palace

claims.text: The Gudigar sandalwood carvers are reported to have come originally from Goa, migrating when early Portuguese invaders tried to convert them forcibly to Christianity.

quotes.quote: The Gudigars are reported to have come originally from Goa, their migration to the towns named above having been occasioned by the attempts of the early Portuguese invaders to convert them forcibly to Christianity.
These are known as gudigars. They claim to have come from Goa

claims.text: Several woodworking communities claim descent from Vishwakarma, among them the barhais of the United Provinces, the asari carvers of Madurai and the suthar kavad makers.

quotes.quote: Traditionally harhais claim descent from Viswakarma, son of Brahma
The carvers of Madurai, Tamil Nadu, known as asaris, claim to be direct descendants of Vishwakarma, the celestial architect.
The suthars choose to use the surname Suthar, and in some cases add Jangid to their name to signify that they are descendants of Vishwakarma

claims.text: The Nizam of Hyderabad commissioned many furniture pieces from Nirmal artisans, and many artisans were invited to set up workshops at Hyderabad in the 1950s.

quotes.quote: The Nizam of Hyderabad is known to have commissioned a large number of furniture pieces from Nirmal artisans over the years, and many artisans were invited to set up workshops at Hyderabad in the 1950s.

claims.text: An account quoted by Thurston tells of an old craftsman at Udayagiri in Nellore district who moved from carving wooden sandals to shaping spoons and forks.

quotes.quote: A modest but interesting industry is carried on at Udayagiri in the Nellore district
In Udayagiri, a village of some note before the days of British rule, there lives an old Muhammadan, who twenty-five years ago used his knife with unusual skill in the manufacture of wooden sandals.
So he tried his hand on the shapening of spoons and forks

claims.text: Watt called the recent Kashmir fashion for realistic walnut carving of water lilies and leaf sprays over tables an unfortunate departure, apparently made to display undercutting.

quotes.quote: Recently in Kashmir a most unfortunate departure has taken place into realistic carving in walnut, in which bunches of water lilies or sprays of
leaves are carved over the surface of tables or other articles, the one object apparently being to display a marvellous degree of undercutting

claims.text: Saharanpur was formerly renowned for its carved shisham doorframes (chaukats), while by Maffey's time its jali trade was entirely in Muslim hands.

quotes.quote: Formerly Sahdranpur was renowned for the excellence of its carved chaukats of shisham wood.
whereas the modern jdli trade is entirely in the hands of Muhammadans.

claims.text: The discovery of aniline dyes and the perfection of chemical dyes ended the cochineal and Indian lac dye trades, leaving lac dye only a very limited market.

quotes.quote: discovery of aniline dyes by Sir W. H. Perkin and others however, and the perfection of chemical dyes in general put an end to the cochineal and Indian lac dye trades, and lac dye has now only a very limited market.

claims.text: Vizagapatam craftsmen had long made chess-tables, jewel cases and boxes in sandal and other woods, veneered with tortoise-shell or bison and buffalo horn.

quotes.quote: Vizagapatam where chess-tables and men, dressing cases, work-boxes, tea-caddies, jewel-cases, glove-boxes, picture-frames, etc., have for many years past been extensively manufactured in sandal and other woods, veneered with tortoise-shell or bison and buffalo-horn

quotes.quote: construction and is the main furniture wood of the country. Its popularity is due to its relatively small coefficient of expansion and contraction, and the fact that it is extremely durable and, practically speaking, immune to insect and fungus attack.

quotes.quote: Sapwood greyish-white ; heartwood light golden brown.

claims.text: Burma and Malabar teak suited construction, while for beauty of grain and figure the dark teak of the Deccan and the Dangs was hard to beat.

quotes.quote: teak from Burma and Malabar are preferable for constructional work, but for beauty of grain and handsome " figure ", the dark coloured timber obtainable from the Deccan and the Dangs is hard to beat.

claims.text: Mysore teak was locally regarded as stronger than Burma teak, a superiority attributed to its close grain and the oil in its pores.

Extremely suitable for chairs, wheel spokes and felloes, sporting requisites, and turnery.

quotes.quote: is recognised as the premier carving wood of India, and Indian sandalwood carvings and small ornamental boxes are famous throughout the world.
album, is used in the well known sandal wood carvings of Mysore, and this wood holds premier place in the world for carved boxes, etc., on account of its pleasant perfume.

claims.text: Mysore recognised four varieties of sandalwood by colour and marking, which depend on the tree's age and locale, the cobra and peacock kinds being best and dearest.

quotes.quote: colour and marking, which depend greatly on its age and locale, four varieties of the wood are recognised :--bili (white), kempu (red), ndga (cobra), and navilu (peacock).
The two latter are the best, and realise the highest prices.

claims.text: Trotter called walnut an excellent wood for carving, much used for that purpose in Kashmir, as well as a valuable furniture wood.

quotes.quote: an excellent wood for carving and is much used for this purpose in Kashmir, in addition to being a valuable furniture wood.

claims.text: In the FAO's Channapatna study, hale wood (Wrightia tinctoria) is the basic raw material of lac-turnery: very close-grained, moderately hard, easily turned, its low oil content aiding the finish.

quotes.quote: The soft wood of the hale tree (Wrightia tinctoria) is first turned into circular shapes

Hale wood is the basic raw material of lac-turnery. It is extremely close grained, moderately hard and easily turned into fine shapes by hand or machine. It has a very low moisture and oil content. The latter helps ensure an excellent finish and translucency after polishing.

claims.text: Channapatna toys are made of ivory wood (Wrightia tinctoria), called hale mara or alae mara in Kannada, a soft, white, fine-grained wood that easily absorbs dyes.

quotes.quote: ivory wood (Wrightia tinctoria) or hale mara in Kannada is the popular choice. Ivory wood is soft, fine grained, white coloured and it easily absorbs dyes, imparting vibrant colours to the toys.
The toys, dolls and other objects manufactured in Channapatna are made of the wood of the ivorywood tree (Wrightia tinctoria), known as hale mara or alae mara in Kannada.

claims.text: At Etikoppaka, figures, miniature temple chariots and boxes were carved from the ivory-coloured ankudu tree (Wrightia tinctoria), the wood found most suitable for toys.

quotes.quote: Figures of gods and goddesses, miniature temple chariots, architectural carvings, boxes, and decorative elements were carved from the ivory colored ankudu tree (Wrightia tinctoria) sourced from nearby forests.
`ankudu' (Wrightea tinctoria) wood is most suitable for making toys.

claims.text: Tirupati carvers mostly used red sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus) from the neighbouring hills and the forests of the Venkatagiri and Kalahasti zamindaris.

quotes.quote: The wood which is most used is red sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus), which is obtained from the neighbouring hills and the forests of the Venkatagiri and Kdlahasti zamindaris.

claims.text: Trotter wrote that carvings, toys and combs were made of any cheap close-grained wood suitable for carving, such as Holarrhena antidysenterica or Wrightia tinctoria.

quotes.quote: Carving , toys , combs } etc.
These are made of any cheap close-grained wood suitable for ^carving such as, Adit a cordifolia, Holarrhena antidysenterica, Boehmeria rugulosa , Wrightia tinctoria , etc.

claims.text: For ornamental turned objects, Watt wrote, light-coloured and uniformly grained woods not liable to warp or split are indispensable.

quotes.locator: Class VI, Division 26, Lac-ware of India, p. 211
quotes.quote: For ornamental objects light coloured and uniformly grained woods, that are not liable to warp or split, are indispensable.

claims.text: Punjab turners worked in shisham and poplar, though at Ferozepore an old pupil of the Mayo School of Art used farásh (Tamarix orientalis) instead.

quotes.quote: Rangata, the polishing stick, &c. The woods used are shisham and poplar.

At Ferozepore, the work of an old pupil of the Mayo School of Art is skilful in execution and artistic in design. He uses the farásh (Tamarix orientalis), and not, as elsewhere, the shisham and poplar

claims.text: Indian inlay was done with other woods, ivory, bone, mother-of-pearl or metals, set either in large pieces or as fine wire.

quotes.quote: accomplished by other woods, by ivory, by bone, by mother-ofpearl or by metals. It may be in large pieces or in fine wire

claims.text: Hoshiarpur inlayers generally used the waste ivory left by the turners of ivory bangles.

quotes.quote: The ivory used is generally the waste stuff left by the turners of ivory bangles

claims.text: Lac is a resinous substance secreted by the lac insect, a member of the scale-insect super-family Coccidae.

quotes.quote: Lac is a resinous .substance secreted by an insect known as the lac insect
Coccidae which is comprised of the .Scale insects and Mealy bugs.

claims.text: Of the lac insects, Laccifer lacca is by far the most important and produces the bulk of the lac of commerce, Glover wrote.

quotes.quote: Laccifer lacca is by far the most important and produces the bulk of the lac of commerce.

claims.text: The resin the lac insects secrete can be processed into shellac, used for jewellery or to finish wooden surfaces, which is why lacquer was originally made with lac.

quotes.quote: The resin secreted by the insects can be processed into shellac. This can be shaped into jewellery or used to finish wooden surfaces, which is why lacquer was originally made with lac.

claims.text: The wood-turning industry demanded superior qualities of lac and preferred pure shellac for its ability to take up colours homogeneously.

quotes.quote: superior qualities are in demand and preference is given to pure shellac on account of its ability to take up colours homogeneously

claims.text: Kavads are built from low-density wood of trees such as mango, semal, adulsa or neem, starting with the primary wooden structure.

quotes.quote: Made from low-density wood from trees such as mango, semal, adulsa or neem, the construction begins with building the primary wooden structure.

claims.text: Sholapith uses the soft white core of the shola plant (Aeschynomene aspera), called pith or Indian cork, to make religious and cultural objects.

quotes.quote: Deriving its name from the plant Aeschynomene aspera, known as shola in Bangla
the soft white core of the shola plant, called pith or Indian cork, is used to make several religious and cultural objects

claims.text: The sholapith craft is also known as netti in Tamil Nadu, the Impart encyclopedia notes.

quotes.quote: The sholapith craft is also known as netti in Tamil Nadu.

claims.text: For cricket bats Salix alba was the best wood, but Salix babylonica was the one most used in India, Trotter wrote.

quotes.quote: Cricket bats.--Salix alba is the best but Salix babylonica is the wood most used for this purpose in India.

claims.text: A distinct class of carpenters cut the printing dies (thappas) for cloth-printers from shisham, mango and ebony, often with delicate and skilful workmanship.

quotes.quote: There is a distinct class of carpenters who earn their living by supplying the cloth-printers (chhipis) with the necessary dies (thappas). These dies are made of shisham, mango, and ebony and are often of delicate and skilful workmanship.

claims.text: Trotter called unseasoned wood the chief stumbling-block to adopting India's lesser-known timbers and said the importance of proper seasoning cannot be over-emphasized.

quotes.quote: The use of unseasonedwood has been the chiefstumbling-block to the adoption of India's lesser known timbers, and the importance of proper seasoning cannot be over-emphasized.

claims.text: Seasoning in the log is negligible: experiments found some species still as moist at the log's centre after 15 to 20 years as when felled.

quotes.locator: Chapter I, Storage of logs, p. 1
quotes.quote: the amount of seasoning which takes place in a log is, to all intents and purposes, negligible, in comparison with the rapid drying which can be effected with converted timber.

quotes.locator: Chapter I, Storage of logs, p. 1
quotes.quote: experiments have shown that, even after 15 to 20 years, some species have the same amount of moisture in the centre of the log as they had when they were felled.

claims.text: Keeping logs under water is storage rather than seasoning, during which sugars, gums and tannins of the sap are leached out of the wood.

quotes.locator: Chapter I, Storage of logs, p. 2
quotes.quote: Water submersion is not a seasoning process, it is merely a method of storage.

quotes.locator: Chapter I, Storage of logs, p. 2
quotes.quote: certain constituents of the sap such as the sugars, gums, and tannins, are leached out of the wood

claims.text: Air-seasoning timber in India depends on two points: proper stacking of the wood and protecting the stack from hot winds, the blazing sun and rain.

quotes.quote: there are two important points to be attended to in air-seasoning timber in India.
The proper piling or stacking of the wood.
The protection of the stack from the prevailing hot winds, the blazing Indian sun, and the rain.

claims.text: C. V. Sweet divided Indian woods into three seasoning classes by how liable they are to crack, split and warp, from refractory to non-refractory woods.

quotes.quote: Mr. C. V. Sweet, late Seasoning Officer at Dehra Dun, has dealt with this question in detail
He divides the Indian woods into three classes
Woods which are only moderately liable to crack, split, and warp, called medium refractory woods.
Woods which are capable ot withstanding rapid seasoning, or are particularly liable to staining, mould, and decay during seasoning, called non-refractory woods.

claims.text: Teak air-seasons easily and quickly with little depreciation when well stacked, and blackwood can be air- or kiln-seasoned without trouble and with little degrade.

quotes.quote: Air-seasons easily, and if properly stacked with a good air circulation, it can be dried quickly with little or no depreciation.
Blackwood can be air-seasoned and kiln-seasoned without trouble and with little degrade.

claims.text: Kiln-seasoning does the work of natural drying in very roughly one-twelfth of the time needed to air-season the same timber, but is expensive on a small scale.

quotes.quote: Kiln-seasoning attempts to carry out exactly the same process as natural drying but in a far shorter period of time ; estimated very roughly at one-twelfth of the time required to air-season the same timber.
Kilnseasoning on a small scale is expensive, owing to the large outlay of capital required to instal seasoning kilns.

claims.text: At Channapatna, hale logs for lac-turnery are cut into billets and seasoned away from heat and sunlight for ten days to a month, depending on the moisture content of the wood.

quotes.quote: The preparation of hale wood for lac-turnery begins with seasoning. Logs are cut into small billets and stored away from heat and sunlight in a location with good air circulation for ten days to a month, depending on the moisture content of the wood.

claims.text: For tarkashi the wood is first seasoned by stacking the planks in air, protected from sunlight and rain, for six to seven months.

quotes.quote: The wood is first seasoned - the planks are stacked and exposed to air, protected from sunlight and rain, for six to seven months.

claims.text: The sandalwood carver draws the design in pencil on the smoothed wood or, for intricate work, glues a paper drawing of the same size onto it.

quotes.quote: proceeds to inscribe the design or pattern by drawing it on the smooth surface of the wood with a pencil. Ifthe design is very intricate, he draws it on a piece of paper of the same size as the slab, and glues it thereon.
The operation is started by either drawing the pattern that is intended to be produced on the smooth and white-washed sandalwood, or on a piece of paper pasted over its surface.

claims.text: The carver engraves the outline of the pattern, roughs out the spaces between the outlines (bosting), then finishes with tools of ever finer edge.

quotes.quote: He then proceeds to mark or engrave the pattern on the wood with an engraver, outlining the design in all its details. The next process is " bosting," or cutting away roughly between the outlines of the pattern
He starts with a large tool, and goes over the work several times with tools of finer and finer edges

claims.text: The Mysore sandalwood carver disdains the file and does his cleanest work with the chisel alone, aided by the wood's fine texture and his very sharp tools.

quotes.quote: A peculiarity of the sandal-wood carver of Mysore is that he disdains a file, and does the cleanest and most finished work with the chisel alone, aided by the fine texture of the wood and the extreme sharpness of his tools.

claims.text: The tools of the Mysore sandalwood carvers were made from European umbrella spokes, ramrods and country steel.

quotes.quote: The tools are made from European umbrella spokes, ramrods, and country steel.

claims.text: A carver needed only a mallet and a dozen small chisels, chiefly flat V chisels (chaursi) and bent round-headed chisels (hirka) for floral patterns.

quotes.locator: Chapter V, Implements and Material, p. 12
quotes.quote: A mallet - usually a plain block of wood - and a dozen small chisels will suffice for all purposes.

quotes.locator: Chapter V, Implements and Material, p. 13
quotes.quote: They fall into two main classes, viz. the flat V chisels known as chaursi; and those with a bent rounded head, used in carving floreated patterns, called hirka.

claims.text: The Punjab turner's lathe (adda) held the wood between spikes on two iron bars and was spun by a bow whose thong looped once round a peg.

quotes.quote: The lath (adda) consists of two iron bars (killa), one fixed in the oround, the other to be adjusted for distance.
On the inner side of each bar isa spike to which the block of wood to be turned (mochha) is attached.
round which the thong of the bow (kaman) is once passed. The bow is worked backwards and forwards, and thus: imparts the necessary rotatory motion.

claims.text: Channapatna lacquerware was traditionally made on hand lathes called patris, turned by a bow string while the turner held the tool in one hand and pressed with his foot.

quotes.quote: Traditionally all lacquerware was produced using simple hand lathes called patris made by local carpenters. A bow string is used to turn a rotating axle in the center of wooden lathe. The turning tool is held in the free hand and pressure is added with the foot, shaping the spinning wood.

claims.text: Production time falls considerably on the electric power lathe because the turner has both hands free for the turning tools.

quotes.quote: The production time decreases considerably on the power lathe as both hands are free to operate turning tools.

claims.text: On the lathe, cutting tools scrape thin continuous chips from the revolving wood, and the shaped piece is sanded smooth while still turning.

quotes.quote: Cutting tools are applied to the revolving piece of wood so that thin continuous chips are scraped off.
Once the desired shape is formed, it is sanded with sandpaper while it is still turning, until the surface is smooth and uniform.

claims.text: In lac-turnery a stick of coloured lac (batti) is pressed against the revolving wood, and the heat of friction melts the lac onto the surface.

quotes.quote: the colour is applied by pressing sticks (batti) of coloured lac to the revolving surface.
a stick of sealing-wax (batti) is pressed against it, as it revolves on the lathe. The heat generated melts the lac and thus colours the wood irregularly.
A lac stick of the chosen colour is pressed to the revolving wood. The friction causes the lac to melt and spread uniformly over the area on which it is applied.
The portion of the lac touching the article melts with the heat generated by friction and colours the wood.

claims.text: A turned article for lac ornament was first polished with a fine powder of broken pottery, which fills up the pores of the wood.

quotes.quote: An article intended to be ornamented with lac is first turned to the desired shape and polished with a fine powder made from broken pottery. This polishing has the effect of filling up the pores.

claims.text: Watt described a cotton rag dipped in sweet oil being held to the revolving object at the end, giving the lac a polish it never subsequently loses.

quotes.quote: Lastly, a cotton rag, dipped in sweet oil (preferably sessanium), is held against the revolving object
the lac takes a polish that it never subsequently loses

claims.text: Channapatna turners buff lacquered pieces with leaves of the screw pine, talegiri (Pandanus odoratissimus), which lends the finish translucency and gloss.

quotes.quote: the lacquered piece is buffed with the leaves of the talegiri (Pandanus odoratissimus)
Final finishing is done using a screw pine leaf to help spread the lac on the turning wood and polish the object. Buffing lends a translucency to the finished product.
which she then buffs to a mirror-like gloss with a long, sharp-edged strip of screw pine leaf, locally called talegiri.

claims.text: Coloured lac sticks are made by heating lac until soft and working colourant into it, with lithophone beaten in at Channapatna until a white tint appears.

quotes.quote: The preparation of lacquer from lac begins with heating and softening.
A specific amount of lithophone is then added to the softened lac and is beaten continuously until a white tint appears.
To prepare the coloured lac sticks, the lac chips are first heated over a coal fire. As they begin melting, dye or colourants are added to the melting lac.
Lacquer pellets are heated slowly in an open oven while the colours and titanium dioxide in powder form are applied to the fluid in small quantity at regular intervals.

claims.text: Punjab turners laid colours in layers and scratched patterns, scraping through black for green, through black and green for red, and to the wood for white.

quotes.quote: Borders are usually made in two or three colours superposed, and the pattern is etched with a chisel
To produce a pattern in green the black is scraped through, for red both the green and black are scraped away, and for white the wood itself is exposed.

claims.text: In etched nakshi work, coats of coloured lac are laid one over another and the surface is scratched with a fine chisel to bring out the colour wanted from below.

quotes.quote: In this class of turnery the object is coated with first one colour, then on the top a second, a third or a fourth, uniformly all over.

With a fine chisel or style the lac-coated Surface is now scratched, the hand being made to move lightly or to press heavily as may be necessary to bring out the colour required from the numerous layers beneath the surface.

claims.text: In inlaying, ivory or bone is cut into thin slips that are laid in place, their outlines scratched on the wood, the spaces cut out and the ivory embedded with glue or cement.

quotes.quote: The ivory or bone is first formed into long strips of a
required shape, then cut transversely into a number of thin shps.
These are laid on their places and the outhnes of the spaces required, scratched on the wood. These are then cut out and the ivory imbedded with glue or other cement as required.

claims.text: Mysore inlayers ornamented the ivory with black designs by scratching a pattern, smearing it with black lac fused by a hot bolt, and scraping off the excess.

quotes.quote: the surface of the ivory is ornamented with black designs. This is accomplished by scratching a pattern on the surface of the ivory, then smearing over with black lakh (lac), fused by means of a hot bolt.
The excess of lakh above the surface is next removed by scraping with the edge of a flat knife.

claims.text: In tarkashi the design is drawn on seasoned shisham, the lines incised, and brass wire laid in the grooves and beaten level with the surface with a hammer.

quotes.quote: The first part of the process of tdrkashi consists of drawing the design in pencil on well-seasoned shisham. The lines are then deeply incised with a sharp knife, and into this brass wire is drawn and beaten down level with the surface of the wood with an iron hammer.
The artisan then lays the wire down on its sharp edge over the groove with one hand, and taps it into place with a hammer held in the other.

claims.text: The dots that fill tarkashi designs, thousands in a few square inches, are minute coils of wire twisted on the point of a needle.

quotes.quote: The dots that diversify the design and soon run up to thousands in a space of only a few inches square, are minute coils of wire twisted up on the point of a needle.
For the decorative dots, thin wire is coiled around the tip of a needle and often beaten directly into the surface.

claims.text: A tarkashi plate twelve inches in diameter occupied a workman for twenty days, Maffey recorded.

quotes.quote: The process requires considerable time and labour. A plate of twelve inches diameter will occupy a workman for twenty days.

claims.text: In sadeli marquetry, thin strips are glued into bundles whose cross-sections show geometric patterns, and slices of these ribbons are glued onto boxes and cabinets.

quotes.quote: These are cut into long thin strips of various shapes and are
glued together in such a manner as to show, on transverse section, geometric patterns of rich and varied design
Thin strips or veneering ribbons are thus made by transverse section on a series of parellel strands and these ribbons are then glued to the surfaces of the boxes, cabinets, etc., as desired.

claims.text: Saharanpur fretwork panels were sawn from a plank already fretted by machine, so one pass of the fret-saw made five or six panels of jali at once.

quotes.quote: The thin panels of fretwork are sawn from a plank previously fretted by machine. In this way one passage of the machine fret-saw is actually doing five or six panels of jdli work at once.

claims.text: Printing blocks carry only part of a design, because cloth-printers use a separate block for applying each colour.

quotes.quote: A separate block is used for the application of each colour: a single block contains only a portion of the design.

claims.text: O'Dwyer recorded Punjab pinjra panels of as many as 2,000 pieces, dowelled together without the assistance of glue and held together by the frame.

quotes.quote: It may consist of as many as 2,000 separate pieces : these are joined together by a process of dowelling without the assistance of glue, the whole being held together by the frame.

claims.text: Scraped stick lac is ground and washed to give seed lac, and shellac is made by melting seedlac or extracting it with a suitable solvent.

quotes.quote: Seed lac is obtained by grinding and washing this stick lac. Shellac is made by melting seedlac or extracting it by a suitable solvent.

claims.text: Stick lac scraped from the branches contains, besides woody matter, the lac resin, lac dye, the bodies of insects and some wax.

quotes.quote: It contains, apart from woody matter, the lac resin, lac dye, bodies of insects and some wax.

claims.text: Lac dye gets its red colour from laccaic acid in the hemolymph, or body fluid, of the lac insect.

quotes.quote: Lac dye gets its red colour from the laccaic acid present in the hemolymph or body fluid of the lac insect.

claims.text: The colouring matter of the insect bodies forms the crimson lac dye when lac is washed, and lac was originally cultivated for this dye.

quotes.quote: It is the colouring matter of the in.sect bodies dead or alive which forms the crimson lac dye when lac is washed. It was for this colouring matter or lac dye, that lac was originally cultivated.

claims.text: Lac dye is extracted by crushing the insects, dissolving the result in an alkaline solution, then acidifying it and adding chalk to settle the dye as sediment.

quotes.quote: It is obtained by separating the insects from the branch and the resin, crushing them and dissolving the result in an alkaline solution. This solution is then acidified and treated with chalk, which reforms the dissolved dye as a sediment.

claims.text: The pigments Indian lac turners used were orpiment, sulphur, white pigments, lead, red mercury, Prussian blue, lamp-black and indigo, Watt recorded.

quotes.quote: The pigments employed are orpiment, sulphur, white pigments, lead, red mercury, prussian blue, lamp-black and indigo.

claims.text: Watt noted that, except for indigo, practically all pigments used in lac and lacquer wares were metallic oxides.

quotes.locator: Class VI, Lac and Lacquer, p. 210
quotes.quote: with the exception of indigo, practically all the other pigments used in the lac and lacquer-wares are metallic oxides.

claims.text: Punjab lac colours were mostly mineral: orpiment for yellow, arsenite of copper for green, red lead or vermilion for red, Prussian blue for blue and lamp-black for black.

quotes.quote: The colours are mostly mineral. Yellow is made with orpiment, green is the arsenite of copper, red with red-lead or vermilion, blue with lájward or Prussian-blue, black with lamp-black.

claims.text: A Punjab yellow lac stick combined a quarter seer of shellac with 2 chitáks of arsenic sulphide (hartál), pounded, warmed and rolled into a cylinder.

quotes.quote: Yellow.-Quarter seer shellac and 2 chitáks sulphide of arsenic (hartál) ;
warming gently, mount the mixture on a stick, cool, and take off the pigment and roll it into a cylinder

claims.text: Watt found aniline dyes almost universally adopted by lac turners, so the delicate colours of old had practically disappeared and new articles faded and tarnished.

quotes.quote: Recently, however, aniline dyes have been almost universally adopted with the result that the delicate artistic colours formerly produced have practically disappeared and the articles made at the present day fade and tarnish

claims.text: Lithophone, a compound of barium sulphate and zinc sulphide, is a white pigment that makes lac lose its transparency and become opaque.

quotes.quote: These include lithophone, a compound of barium sulphate and zinc sulphide which is a white pigment that enables lac to lose its transparency and become opaque.

claims.text: Channapatna lac sticks were coloured with aniline colours including rhodamine for rose and auramine for yellow, plus diamond green, purple, violet and red.

quotes.quote: Equally important are aniline colours which are used to prepare lac sticks. The following basic colours are used: rhodamine (rose), auromine (yellow), diamond green, purple, violet and red.

claims.text: Teak can be kiln-seasoned, but surface oxidation tends to discolour the wood, which proper treatment avoids.

quotes.quote: Can be kiln-seasoned, but care is needed as surface oxidization is apt to discolour the wood. This can, however, be avoided by proper treatment without difficulty.

claims.text: In atishi or fire work, a paste of tinfoil and glue under a layer of red or yellow lac gives the turned object a rich fiery glow.

quotes.quote: it receives a coating of finely divided tinfoil made into a -paste with glue
Over the top of the tin, a layer of red or yellow lac is next given, with the result that the object obtains a rich fiery glow.

claims.text: Timber grain shaped Indian carving: deep undercutting was possible in teak, redwood and walnut, low relief suited shisham and deodar, ebony took incised designs and sandal minute detail.

quotes.quote: The art conceptions seen in wood-work have been greatly influenced by the grain of the timber employed, such as the deep under-cutting and sculpture that is possible with teik, red-wood and walnut
the low relief of shisham and deodar, the incised designs of ebony, the intricate and minute details of sandal

claims.text: Teak shrinks less than other timbers and its natural oil slows the absorption of moisture, so it responds slowly to changing weather.

quotes.quote: the shrinkage of teak is less than the shrinkage of other timbers, and as a result, the " working " or " moving " of teak is slight.

the natural oil in teak wood retards the absorption of moisture, and, as a result, when teak is exposed to fluctuating weather conditions, it takes longer to respond to these conditions than other woods.

claims.text: Walnut is light yet extremely tough, hard and elastic, and once dried it does not shrink, swell or split excessively in damp, wet or heat.

quotes.quote: It is a relatively light wood, of extreme toughness, hardness, and elasticity, working easily and finishing to a fine surface.
when once dried, it is not liable to shrink, swell, or split excessively when exposed to damp, wet or heat.

claims.text: Walnut seasons slowly and shrinks considerably while drying, and large walnut planks are rather liable to split down the middle.

quotes.quote: Walnut wood seasons slowly and shrinks considerably while doing so
although large planks are rather liable to split down the middle.

claims.text: Sandalwood is highly scented, close-grained and tough, and the fineness and evenness of its structure make it capable of the most delicate carving.

quotes.quote: The wood is highly scented, close-grained and tough, and, from the fineness and evenness of its structure, is capable of the most delicate carving.

claims.text: Because of the extreme hardness of Nagina's ebony the carving is never deep, and undercutting is never practised.

quotes.quote: Owing to the extreme hardness of the wood the carving is never deep. It is strictly Muhammadan in character and under-cutting is never practised.

claims.text: Carving a figure in wood is harder than in marble or stone because wood cracks easily, is damaged by insects and suffers from changes in the atmosphere.

quotes.quote: To carve a figure in wood is more difficult than sculpting with marble or stone, owing to wood tending to crack easily, to be damaged by insects, or to suffer from changes in the atmosphere.

claims.text: The hardness of sheesham helps it hold the tension that keeps a pinjra panel's pieces together in the frame, making it particularly suited to the craft.

quotes.quote: The pieces are held together by the resultant tension within the frame
The hardness of sheesham helps the wood hold tension better, making it particularly suited to this craft.

claims.text: Tarkashi prefers shisham because its dense, coarse grain holds the inlay in place and its dark, oily wood sets off the metal by contrast.

quotes.quote: Tarkashi is done preferably on locally sourced shisham (North Indian rosewood, Dalbergia sissoo), whose dense grain and coarseness help hold the inlay in place; its dark colour, due to its high oil content, also brings out the metal inlay by contrast.

claims.text: In Chiniot's brass inlay, laid on and held by nails, the slightest warp in the wood was fatal, because the brass bulged up at once.

quotes.quote: The brass inlay of Chiníot is superior to that of Hoshiárpur in design and in finish.
speaking, inlaid, but rather laid on, and are retained in their place by the nails.
The slightest warp in the wood is fatal to the effect, for the, brass ab once bulges up, and is not readily smoothed down again.

claims.text: The Udayagiri craftsman was unable to make his boxes during the hot months, because the wood cracked under the knife.

quotes.quote: He is unable to make the boxes, which he turns out, during the hot months, as the wood cracks under the knife

claims.text: Maffey contrasted Hindu carving, as a rule deeply undercut and fantastic, with Muhammadan carving, which used geometric diapers and flat relief.

quotes.quote: In Muhammadan wood-carving the place of fantastic Hindu ornamentation is filled by a free use of geometric diapers ; and whereas Hindu work is as a rule deeply undercut, Muhammadan work is marked by flatness of relief.

claims.text: The Deputy Commissioner of Fyzabad, quoted by Maffey, held that leaving no space uncarved is typically Indian, unlike the bold ornament on plain ground of Chinese and Japanese work.

lede.text: India's wood crafts ornament wood by carving, inlaying, veneering, painting and lacquering, in architecture, furniture and cabinet work, while village turners made toys, nests of boxes, bed-posts and other turned ware.
Watt held that the grain of each timber shaped the style, from deep undercutting in teak, redwood and walnut to low relief in shisham and deodar and minute detail in sandal.
Its makers include carpenters and carvers who claim descent from Vishwakarma, the Gudigars, who say they were temple carvers and painters, and the kharádi turners whom Watt found in every village.

Centres include Kashmir's walnut work, Saharanpur and Nagina carving, Mysore's Gudigar sandal carvers, and lac-turning at Channapatna and Etikoppaka, and an EPCH presentation counts around 1.1 million artisans living by wooden handicrafts.

sentences.text: Wood traditionally made house posts, rafters, yokes, ploughs, toys, planks and furniture, and the Salar Jung Museum calls wood carving an ancient art of India.
The village turner with his lathe prepared toys, nests of boxes, bed-posts and hookah mouthpieces, and Watt called lac-turnery an essentially Indian craft.
The FAO study defines lac-turnery as turning wood on the lathe, which yields the lacquered wooden items known as lacquerware around Channapatna.

Watt found inlaying rarely practised by itself, with designs like those of carving, though a few centres were long reputed for expert inlayers, and tarkashi inlays thin metal wire on shisham and other hardwood.
Sholapith uses the soft white core of the shola plant, called pith or Indian cork, and the craft is also known as netti in Tamil Nadu.
A distinct class of carpenters cut printing dies (thappas) of shisham, mango and ebony for cloth-printers, and Salix babylonica was the wood most used for cricket bats in India.

Registered geographical indications include Bastar Wooden Craft (2008), the Wooden Mask of Kushmandi (2018), Kallakurichi Wood Carving (2021), the Chamoli Wooden Ramman Mask and Uttarakhand Likhai (2023) and Wancho Wooden Craft (2024).

Tamil Nadu released GI certificates for Kallakurichi and Arumbavur wood carving and Thanjavur pith work in 2021, and Arumbavur carving, native to Perambalur district, draws on temple architecture and uses siris, mango, rosewood and neem.
The Salar Jung Museum's story says Ashoka's palace at Pataliputra and the grand temple at Bodh Gaya were made in wood, and that the Rigveda names the woodworker sutradhar.
The sixth-century Brihat Sanhita lists sal, sandalwood and teak among the woods most esteemed for furniture, and the Silpa Sastra and Puranas set rules for selecting and felling trees.
Pinjra latticework appears in records of Akbar's reign (1556-1605), and the Ain-i-Akbari suggests it was by then highly developed and valued.
Lac was known from at least the first millennium BCE, and its name comes from the Sanskrit laksha, meaning 100,000, for the many insects needed to make the resin.
Thrones and state chairs were made from the most ancient times, but chairs and sofas were a modern introduction, and European ideas of comfort created a demand for household furnishing.
Wood-carving was first started at the Madras School of Arts in 1877 in a desultory way, and the department ornamented European furniture, mostly in teak and blackwood.
Maffey judged that no craft had suffered more than wood-carving, which in Lower Bengal was practically extinct.
The News Minute reports that Arumbavur's carvers, mostly of the Boyar community, trace their origins to Madurai and once travelled to build temple cars.

Watt listed teak, shisham, deodar, sandalwood, ebony and walnut first among ornamental woods, approximately by importance, and the Salar Jung Museum's story names teak, blackwood, rosewood, sandalwood, mahogany, ebony, mango and neem.
Trotter called teak the main furniture wood of India, durable and practically immune to insects and fungus, and rosewood probably the finest furniture wood India possesses.
Maffey called shisham the wood par excellence for all carving and Trotter the best chair wood, while soft, easily worked tun was the staple timber of cabinet-makers, notably in Saharanpur district.
Watt called sandalwood the most popular and most expensive of all woods, Trotter called it the premier carving wood of India, and Trotter found walnut much used for carving in Kashmir.
The so-called ebony of the Nagina carvers is Diospyros tomentosa, a black and heavy heartwood imported from Central India.
The lac-turners of Channapatna and Etikoppaka use ivory wood (Wrightia tinctoria), soft, white and fine-grained, which easily absorbs dyes.
Lac is a resinous substance secreted by the lac insect, which Impart names Kerria lacca and Glover Laccifer lacca, and shellac made from it is used to finish wooden surfaces.
Inlay used other woods, ivory, bone, mother-of-pearl or metals, and Hoshiarpur's inlayers took the waste ivory left by the turners of ivory bangles.
Trotter stressed proper seasoning, found some logs as moist at the centre after 15 to 20 years as when felled, and put kiln-seasoning at very roughly one-twelfth of the air-seasoning time.
Air-seasoning timber in India depends on proper stacking and on protecting the stack from hot winds, the blazing sun and rain.
Channapatna turners season hale billets for ten days to a month, depending on the moisture content of the wood, and tarkashi workers air their planks for six to seven months.
The sandalwood carver draws or pastes the design on the wood, engraves its outline, roughs out the spaces between (bosting) and finishes with tools of finer and finer edge.
A coloured lac stick pressed against the revolving wood melts with the heat of friction, and at Channapatna the piece is buffed with screw pine (talegiri) leaves for translucency.
Gujarat's craft portal says Sankheda furniture is made by turning teak pieces on a lathe, applying powdered tin in a solvent, lacquering and leaf-polishing them, then assembling the furniture.
In tarkashi, brass wire is laid in lines incised in seasoned shisham and beaten level, and its dots are minute coils of wire twisted on the point of a needle.
Sadeli marquetry glues thin strips into bundles whose cross-sections show geometric patterns, and ribbons cut from them are glued onto boxes and cabinets.
Stick lac contains lac resin, lac dye, insect bodies and some wax, and the red of lac dye comes from laccaic acid in the insect's body fluid.

Sources differ on lac pigments: Watt called practically all but indigo metallic oxides, yet listed sulphur, red mercury and lamp-black, and O'Dwyer gives the Punjab yellow as arsenic sulphide (hartál).
O'Dwyer found Punjab lac colours mostly mineral: orpiment for yellow, arsenite of copper for green, red lead or vermilion for red, Prussian blue and lamp-black.
Aniline dyes, almost universally adopted by Watt's time, made the delicate colours of old practically disappear and new articles fade and tarnish.
At Channapatna lithophone, a compound of barium sulphate and zinc sulphide, makes lac opaque, and aniline colours such as rhodamine and auramine tint the sticks.
In atishi work a paste of tinfoil under a layer of red or yellow lac gives the turned object a rich fiery glow.
Watt held that grain shaped Indian carving, allowing deep undercutting in teak, redwood and walnut, low relief in shisham and deodar and minute detail in sandal.
Teak shrinks less than other timbers and its oil slows the absorption of moisture, and walnut, once dried, does not shrink, swell or split excessively.
The fineness and evenness of sandalwood make it capable of the most delicate carving, while the extreme hardness of Nagina's ebony keeps its carving never deep.
Carving a figure in wood is harder than in stone because wood cracks easily, is damaged by insects and suffers from changes in the atmosphere.
The hardness of sheesham helps it hold the tension that keeps a pinjra panel's pieces together, and at Chiniot the slightest warp in the wood made laid-on brass inlay bulge.
At Udayagiri the wood cracked under the knife during the hot months, so the craftsman was unable to make his boxes then.
Maffey contrasted deeply undercut Hindu carving with Muhammadan carving in geometric diapers and flat relief, and an officer he quoted held that leaving no space uncarved is typically Indian.
Gudigar carvers entirely cover boxes and desks with interlacing foliage and scroll work, leaving not the smallest portion of the wood untouched.
In the Panjab a carved door was a sign of position and wealth, and the most common Indian door turns on pivots instead of hinges.

Khatamband, geometric pine panelling for ceilings, was a speciality of Kashmir, and pinjrakari is framed latticework whose parts are joined without adhesive, though artisans today also use nails and glue.
Madras School of Arts furniture joined the cabinet-maker's structure to Dravidian ornament, and Madurai is famous for blackwood tables with legs of elephant heads or yali figures.
Ornamental lacquering includes abri or cloud work, atishi or fire work, nakshi or pattern work and tin-foil decoration.
A kavad opens like a shrine through hinged painted panels, and Savantvadi woodwork was painted in oil with turned, lac-coloured feet.
Temple cars of South India have exquisite woodwork, richly carved with deities and scroll-work.

In Mysore, sandalwood carving was confined to a few Gudigar families in the Sorab and Sagar taluks of Shimoga district, and Watt's other chief centres included Travancore, Trichinopoly, Tirupati, Madura, Surat, Ahmedabad and Bombay.
EPCH links Srinagar with walnut and deodar woodcraft, Saharanpur with carved furniture and screens, and Nagina with carved boxes.

Watt's centres of superior plain lac-ware included Patna, Murshidabad, Sylhet, Agra, Lucknow, Benares and Mirzapur as well as Hoshiarpur, Jodhpur, Savantvadi, Bangalore and Channapatna, though practically every town had its lac turners.
Watt's chief inlay centres included Hoshiarpur, Jalandhar and Chiniot in the Panjab, Mainpuri, Nagina, Monghyr, Nepal, and Mysore, where ivory was set in shisham, rosewood or ebony.
Mainpuri remains a major tarkashi centre whose work is considered the finest; Nagina, Pilakhuwa, Saharanpur district and Jaipur are others.
Pinjra work survives in Srinagar, Anantnag, Badgam, Baramula, Kupwara and Rajouri in Kashmir and in Amritsar in Punjab.
Kavad-making is primarily concentrated in Bassi in Chittorgarh, and the Naqash artisans of Nirmal and Hyderabad apply Nirmal painting's lacquered finish to figurines and furniture.
As of 2022, lac was cultivated mainly in Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, Odisha and West Bengal.
India's wooden handicraft exports were worth US$584.09 million in 2016-17, and an EPCH presentation says wooden handicrafts give a livelihood to around 1.1 million artisans.
In a 2016 estimate, teak made up 50% of the timber of the Indian furniture industry, with mahogany, cedar, sheesham, mango and others at 30%.
Maffey found that carving European articles de luxe in the workshops of Hoshiarpur, Jalandhar, Nagina and Saharanpur employed few workmen at a high rate of profit.
Saharanpur's fretted tun-wood trade prospered by giving tourists portable mementos, and Panjab redwood tables were exported by shiploads to Europe and America.

Sandal was long a state monopoly yielding the largest portion of Mysore's forest revenue, and Down To Earth reported Karnataka's sandalwood output falling from 3,000 tonnes in 1977-1978 to 20 tonnes in 2002.
Down To Earth reported that with a total ban on ivory most ivory craftspeople turned to camel and buffalo bone or sandalwood.
In November 2022, according to MoEFCC, the fall in exports of shisham products had affected the livelihoods of around 50,000 artisans.
Sankheda's Kharadi craftsmen still make furniture for rituals, weddings and celebrations, while younger craftsmen produce furniture for urban markets.

Mysore's first forest conservancy reserved teak and sandal, the rising price of red sanders drove Tirupati carvers to pala (Wrightia tinctoria), and Nirmal's artisans replaced dwindling Tella Poniki with teak.
The environment ministry said in 2023 that red sanders is listed in CITES Appendix II since 1994 with a zero quota for wild exports, and it rejoined the IUCN's endangered list in 2021.
Karnataka's Forest (Amendment) Act 2001 recognised sandalwood growers as owners without diluting state control, and a 1969 Jammu and Kashmir act imposed a blanket ban on cutting walnut trees.
The Supreme Court records that Act 28 of 1986 restricted trade in wild animals and trophies and Act 44 of 1991 totally prohibited trade in imported ivory.
EPCH says CITES listed all Dalbergia, including rosewood and sheesham, in Appendix II in 2016, though Down To Earth dates the listing to 2017, and exporters then needed CITES permits.
India entered a reservation with a note received on 27 December 2016, and MoEFCC authorised EPCH to issue Vriksh Shipment Certificates in lieu of CITES permits, the first on 27 February 2017.

CoP18 rejected the proposal to delete Dalbergia sissoo from Appendix II in 2019, and at the 19th Conference of Parties in 2022 India's proposal again failed but shisham items each under 10 kg were exempted from permits.
Lac insects live on host trees such as the Indian jujube, kusum and palash, and are cultivated by tying an infested branch to a tree.
A 2026 review of 55 studies in the National Medical Journal of India says its evidence suggests that workers exposed to wood dust have reduced lung function.
The review notes that several systematic reviews have established an association between wood dust exposure and upper respiratory tract cancers.
In Kerala, 150 carpenters with at least 5 years of wood dust exposure showed significantly reduced lung function compared with 150 matched healthy controls.
